sources.entry: Flipping out, Flickr. One of the first articles about feature flags.

summary.title: Flipping Out
summary.one_liner: Flickr's account of using feature flags (per-environment) and feature flippers (per-user) to ship unbranched, continuously integrated code.
takeaways: Flickr keeps all code on a single head branch and deploys it to production several times a day.
Feature flags let the same codebase behave differently per environment, so a launch can be a config change from false to true.
Feature flippers enable unfinished features for individual users, so developers can test without affecting others.
Integrating all code as soon as it is committed removes merge work and leads to smaller, more frequent deploys with easier bug fixing.
Drawbacks: flagged code is restricted to the dev team, and old versions must be removed after launch.
summary.summary: The article explains how Flickr avoids long-lived branches by keeping all code on head and deploying it often. Feature flags are config values checked in code (for example, enable_unicorn_polo) that are set differently in each environment, so finished code can be turned on by flipping a single value. Feature flippers extend this to per-user control, letting developers test in-progress features in isolation. The author notes the tradeoffs: the approach is limited to the dev team because flagged code can cause serious harm, and old code paths must be cleaned up after launch.
